title: Citroën 2CV elektrikli konseptiyle geri dönüyor: Üretim 2028'de
summary: Citroën, ikonik modeli 2CV'yi Paris Otomobil Fuarı'nda tanıttığı elektrikli konseptle yeniden canlandırıyor. Seri üretim versiyonunun 2028'de yollara çıkması hedefleniyor.
body:
Fransız otomotiv üreticisi Citroën, efsanevi klasiği 2CV modelini modern çağa uyarlayan **Citroën 2CV elektrikli** konseptini Paris Otomobil Fuarı'nda sergiledi. Şirketin paylaştığı bilgilere göre, konseptin seri üretim versiyonunun 1948 yılındaki ilk tanıtımından tam 80 yıl sonra, 2028 yılının sonlarında satışa sunulması planlanıyor.

## Citroën 2CV elektrikli konsepti neler sunuyor?

Yeni model, orijinal tasarımın karakteristik çizgilerini modern hatlarla bir araya getiriyor. Ayrık yuvarlak farlar, kavisli tavan çizgisi, katlanabilir kumaş tavan ve basamaklı kaput gibi nostaljik unsurlar konseptte korunuyor. 3,76 metre uzunluğundaki araç, orijinal modelden daha kısa boyutlara sahip ve Citroën ürün gamında Ami ile C3 arasına konumlanıyor. 

İç mekânda ise abartılı ekranlar yerine sade bir yerleşim tercih ediliyor. 8 inçlik kare bilgi-eğlence ekranı, dışarı çıkarılabilen taşınabilir hoparlör ve piknik için sökülebilen koltuklar kabinde yer alıyor. Orijinal modelin engebeli tarlalarda yumurtaları kırmadan taşıma şartnamesine atıfta bulunularak kapı ceplerine yumurtalık bölmeleri eklenmiş durumda.

## Ağırlık hedefi ve çıkış takvimi

Citroën, aracın motor gücü, batarya kapasitesi veya menzil verilerini henüz açıklamadı. Ancak batarya boyutunu makul tutabilmek adına hedeflenen boş ağırlığın yaklaşık 1.000 kilogram olduğu belirtiliyor. Şirket, Avrupa pazarında yaklaşık 15 bin avroluk bir başlangıç fiyatı hedefliyor; modelin Türkiye satış planı ve fiyatı ise henüz duyurulmadı.

**Neden önemli?** Avrupa pazarında artan uygun fiyatlı şehir içi elektrikli otomobil rekabetinde Citroën, nostaljik tasarımını hafif ve erişilebilir bir gövdeyle birleştirerek geniş kitlelere hitap etmeyi amaçlıyor.
visual_scene: A minimalist studio composition showing a sculptural curved metal vehicle panel finished in vibrant orange-red lacquer, resting beside a smoothly carved wooden egg in an eggcup made of raw terracotta.
meta_description: Citroën 2CV elektrikli konsepti Paris'te tanıtıldı. Nostaljik çizgileri koruyan hafif şehir otomobilinin 2028'de yollara çıkması hedefleniyor.
image_alt: Canlı turuncu-kırmızı kavisli metal panel ve yanında duran ahşap yumurta heykeliyle yeni Citroën konseptini temsil eden…
carousel_points: İkonik Fransız modeli 2CV, modern elektrikli şehir aracı konsepti olarak yeniden tanıtıldı.
Yaklaşık bir ton ağırlık hedeflenen aracın seri üretiminin 2028'de gelmesi planlanıyor.
Kapı ceplerindeki yumurtalıklar ve katlanır kumaş tavan orijinal modele sadık kalıyor.
triage_reason: Efsanevi Citroen 2CV elektrikli olarak geri dönüyor.

source_texts.title: Citroen’s 2CV is Back, And It’s Still A Safe Space For Eggs
source_texts.summary: 2 CV Concept revealed at the Paris Motor Show becomes €15,000 production reality by 2028
source_texts.text:
- Citroen is taking on cut-price Chinese EVs with a homage to the iconic 2CV.
- A production version of the retro 2 CV Concept hits showrooms in late 2028.
- In-door egg storage nods to the original 2CV’s quirky egg-friendly design brief.
The Mini Cooper, Fiat 500, VW Beetle, Renault 5, Chevy Camaro, and other classics have been resurrected to push our nostalgia buttons over the last 30 years. But the Citroën 2CV was always a glaring absentee from the list, until this week’s Paris Motor Show. This is the 2 CV Concept, and it’s more than a bit fun. A production version arrives in 2028, Citroën promises.
Previous Citroën CEOs vowed they’d never resurrect the iconic 2CV, despite it remaining the brand’s most famous car. More than 3.8 million were sold between 1948 and 1990. But now Citroën, like other legacy brands, is making use of its heritage to remind us why we should stick with it as Chinese automakers take an ever larger slice of the European car market.
The result is a four-door electric hatch concept that doesn’t just dip its toe in retro waters. It free dives right to the bottom. All the classic design cues are present. The plunging, ribbed hood, the bug-eye headlights on fenders that stand proud of the flat bodywork, and the roll-back canvas roof. But there’s a pumped-up muscular look this time around, and the wide track and 19-inch wheels fill the fenders like no original 2CV ever did.
It’s also around 8 inches (0.2 m) smaller than the OG tin snail, at 148 inches ( 3.76 m) long. Citroën says that size makes it easy to park in cities, but it will also help keep the cost of the production version down to just €15,000 ($16.8k / £12.7k).
Removable Seats, Egg Storage
The interior definitely doesn’t scream ‘budget car,’ even if it does channel the simplicity of the original. The bench seats can be removed for picnics, and a portable hamper on the floor serves as a console and storage cubby. The doors even have an integral egg box. Why? Because the original 1930s design brief for the 2CV called for a car that could carry a basket of eggs across a rutted field without any breakages.
Other retro details include a single-spoke steering wheel and transmission shifter that sprouts from under the dash. But that shifter is hooked up to an electric drivetrain here, not an air-cooled 2-cylinder and four-speed manual.
Citroën hasn’t revealed anything about the motor and battery. But it’s unlikely to be fast, or go far on a charge. The target price makes it impossible. Rival Renault’s base model Twingo produces 81 hp (82 PS / 60 kW) and lasts 163 miles (262 km), which might offer some kind of guide. We’ll find out more in the run up to the production 2CV making its global debut at the 2028 Paris Motor Show, exactly after the original premiered at the same event.

source_texts.title: The Citroën 2CV Is Back As An Ultra-Affordable City Car
source_texts.summary: The new Citroën 2CV is packed with clever retro touches and could become one of Europe's cheapest EVs when it arrives in 2028.
source_texts.text:
The Citroën 2CV Is Back As An Ultra-Affordable City Car
The new Citroën 2CV is packed with clever retro touches and could become one of Europe's cheapest EVs when it arrives in 2028.
Fiat set the template with the 500, and Renault followed with the latest Twingo. Now, Citroën wants in on the retro city-car revival with a modern take on one of France’s most recognizable cars: the 2CV.
Known affectionately as the "Duck," or "La Deuche" in France, the 2CV is making a comeback at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. And judging by the concept, Citroën isn't simply trying to copy the original.
Citroën's goal was to create a small EV that's practical and inexpensive, but something that still feels special to drive. The production car would slot between the tiny Ami and the C3 in Citroën's lineup.
Despite its modern technology, the 2CV Concept is actually smaller than the original. It measures about 147.6 inches (3.7 meters) long, compared to the roughly 151.2 inches (3.8 meters) of the original 2CV.
Citroën says keeping the dimensions compact was intentional. The idea was to bring back the light, playful nature of small cars while making the vehicle easy to drive and park in crowded cities.
The target weight is around 2,200 pounds, too. Keeping the car light means Citroën doesn't need an enormous battery to provide useful everyday range. That should also help keep the purchase price and running costs down.
Despite its modern technology, the 2CV Concept is actually smaller than the original.
The concept takes the same minimalist approach to its construction. Broad, flat body panels, simple air intakes below the windshield, and separate bumpers that can be replaced individually are all designed to make the car easier and cheaper to build and repair.
Citroën is also working with Michelin on a “universal digital tire twin,” which is designed to monitor tire health and continuously adapt the vehicle's behavior based on road and environmental conditions.
The design is where the connection to the original 2CV is most obvious. The concept has the same basic proportions and rounded silhouette, but Citroën has tightened up the details for the modern era. There's a steep windshield, a gently curved roof, prominent fenders, and relatively simple body surfacing.
Up front are freestanding round headlights paired with a modern LED light signature. The hood also incorporates a reference to the historic TPV project—the “Toute Petite Voiture,” or “very small car”—that eventually became the 2CV.
There are also some deliberately old-school touches, including exposed windshield wipers and air openings integrated into the front end.
From the side, the concept gets more playful. The door handles take inspiration from the original 2CV, while slim turn signals sit in the rear roof pillars. The 19-inch steel wheels are another modern interpretation of a classic design.
The rear is arguably the most distinctive part of the car, with a curved roofline, black tailgate extending down into the bumper, and horizontal LED lighting elements. Even the license plate is a little Easter egg, with the various nicknames given to the 2CV around the world.
Citroën isn't trying to turn the 2CV into another screen-filled EV, either.
The interior is bright and open, with wide seats featuring the company's Advanced Comfort technology. The passenger seat can slide outward, while removable storage baskets and soft strap-style door handles add some useful practicality.
Instead of a conventional dashboard, the driver gets a minimalist control setup centered around a cylindrical structure. It houses the steering wheel, control stalks, shift paddle, and Citroën Smart Vision Display, which projects important information into the driver's line of sight.
There's also an 8.0-inch square touchscreen that combines digital functions with physical controls. Its graphics are inspired by comic books, adding a little personality to what could otherwise be a very basic interface.
Then there's “Radioën,” a removable radio that doubles as a portable speaker. You can take it out of the car and bring the music with you, which is neat.
A fabric folding roof is another obvious nod to the original 2CV, giving the cabin a more open and airy feel. The elaborate string of lights around the interior, however, probably isn't making the transition to production.
The 2CV Concept is filled with tons of little references to the original. The exterior is finished in a color called “Infra Red,” combining orange, yellow, and red tones as a nod to the classic 2CV Spot. Inside, the seats feature a modern take on the old 2CV's checkered upholstery.
There are also beige Bakelite-inspired elements throughout the cabin. Bakelite was one of the first fully synthetic plastics and was used for various components on early 2CVs. Wood, textured fabrics, wicker-inspired materials, and 3D-printed storage baskets give the interior a warmer, more tactile feel than the typical modern EV cabin.
Even the pedals get in on the joke; a turtle represents the brake, while a hare marks the accelerator.
The door pockets are another clever callback. They're designed to carry eggs, referencing one of the famous requirements from the original 2CV's development brief. The horn and electric motor sounds reference the original car, while the ventilation flaps beneath the windshield and umbrella-handle-style selector mimic familiar 2CV details.
The numbers 48, 90, and 26 on the windshield represent the original car's launch year, the end of its production run, and the year of this concept's debut.
Citroën says the production version will be built in Europe and is targeting a starting price of around €15,000 (or around $16,000 at current conversion rates). That would make it one of the more affordable ways to get into an electric car, assuming Citroën can keep the final price anywhere close to that target.
The production model is expected to arrive by 2028, potentially making its debut at the 2028 Paris Motor Show. If that happens, the timing would be perfect: exactly 80 years after the original 2CV first appeared.
Of course, not everything on this concept will survive the trip to production, but if Citroën can preserve the basic formula—a lightweight, inexpensive, practical EV with plenty of personality—the 2CV could be one of the more interesting entries in Europe's growing crop of affordable electric city cars.

source_texts.title: Citroen Is Finally Bringing Back The 2CV. And I’m Here For It
source_texts.summary: The electric concept channels the original’s charm and previews a European-built production car targeting a €15,000 starting price.
source_texts.text:
Citroen Is Finally Bringing Back The 2CV. And I’m Here For It
The electric concept channels the original’s charm and previews a European-built production car targeting a €15,000 starting price.
- Citroën’s electric 2CV concept previews a European-built production car targeted at around €15,000 by 2028.
- It’s slightly shorter than the new Renault Twingo and aims to undercut its price by roughly €4,500.
- Retro styling meets a one-ton weight target, but battery size, range and charging speeds remain undisclosed.
Renault is proving that nostalgia sells electric cars. Its new 5 and Twingo are getting good reviews and finding plenty of buyers. Citroën has a 2CV-shaped hole in its lineup, and it’s finally addressing it.
This is the Citroën 2CV Concept, set to debut at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. It brings back the familiar shape of the little French icon, swaps combustion for electricity, and previews a production car due by 2028.
Making an expensive car that reminds people of a cheap one is easy enough. But to stay true to the original 2CV, the reborn EV will be very affordable. Citroën wants to build it in Europe and sell it from around €15,000.
It would even undercut the new Renault Twingo E-Tech. That car launched with a French starting price of €19,490 before incentives, putting Citroën’s target roughly €4,500 lower. We still need the fine print on the 2CV’s price, including whether it includes any subsidies (up to €5,700 in France), but the ambition is clear.
They’re almost exactly the same size, too. The Citroën is 3.76 meters (148 inches) long, making it just three centimeters (just over an inch) shorter than the Twingo. It’s also shorter than the original 2CV and would fit between the Ami and C3 in its lineup.
Citroën is aiming for a weight of around 1,000 kilograms (2,205 pounds). Keeping the weight down means it can have a smaller battery, which will help keep it affordable. That’s the thinking, anyway. The future production model’s battery capacity, range, charging speeds, and power output haven’t been announced.
The styling leans into what people remember about the old 2CV: separate round headlight pods, pronounced fenders, an upright windshield, and that iconic curved roof. The hood in particular takes inspiration from the TPV, the project that previewed the original car.
On paper, that sounds like the right approach. The 2CV had such an unusual shape that Citroën doesn’t need to pile on decorative references to make the connection. Keeping those proportions while tightening up the lines should do most of the work.
What surprised me were the concept's 19-inch wheels. They’re steel wheels, which feels right for a 2CV, but that’s still a lot of wheel for something supposed to be simple and cheap, although they will likely shrink for production.
The other exterior details include exposed wipers, air inlets below the windshield, and slim turn signals integrated into the rear roof pillars. It has a contrasting black tailgate that stretches down to the bumper, plus very modern-looking LED lights.
Inside, Citroën has tried to make the small cabin feel open by removing almost the entire dashboard. A cylindrical assembly holds the steering wheel, controls, and a “Smart Vision Display” that projects information into the driver’s field of view. There’s also a square eight-inch touchscreen with comic-inspired graphics, plus physical controls.
The broad seats use Citroën’s Advanced Comfort technology, and the passenger seat extends so you can stretch out during a stop. You also get a folding fabric roof, removable storage baskets, a removable speaker, and fabric door-pull straps.
Gallery: Citroën 2CV Concept (2026)
Citroën says door pockets are even designed to carry eggs, a nod to the original car’s famous design brief.
To bring this car to market at this price, Citroën is getting help from the European Union. The manufacturer says the production model will be designed to meet future European E-Car rules. The European Commission has proposed an M1E category for electric cars up to 4.2 meters long, aiming to freeze regulatory requirements for ten years. The idea is to give manufacturers a more predictable, less costly route to building affordable EVs.
What I really like about this reborn 2CV is that it arrives at a time when car prices have skyrocketed. Like the original, the new EV will give people a way to get around when more expensive cars are out of reach. If Citroën can do that again, the familiar face will just be a bonus.
